title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team
rating: R (Strong Sexual Content, Graphic Violence, Nudity)

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma does not qualify as a woke trapp under VVWS. A woke trap requires the film to pretend to be apolitical or traditional before revealing its ideology. This film is overt about its ideological commitments from the first frame. The trans-ghost villain, the queer filmmaker protagonst, the polyamory, and the meta-commentary on 'fixing' a 'transphobic' franchise are all foregrounded. No bat-and-switch.

director.name: Jane Schoenbrun
director.ideology: WOKE. Schoenbrun is a trans filmmaker whose entire filmography is explicitly about trans identity and queer experience. Their previous film I Saw the TV Glow (2024) was a trans allegory set in a 1990s television fandom. We're All Going to the World's Fair (2021) explored online identity formation through a trans lens. Schoenbrun is not hiding their ideology. It is the subject of their work.
director.profile: Jane Schoenbrun (born 1987) is a non-binary filmmaker from New York whose work occupies the intersection of horror, internet culture, and trans identity. Their films treat genre frameworks as vehicles for exploring dysphoria, dissociation, and queer desire. Camp Miasma is their most commercially accessible work yet, backed by Brad Pitt's Plan B and released through Mubi. It premiered at Cannes 2026 where it won the Queer Palm. Schoenbrun's artistic project is consistent and legible: use horror's vocabulary of bodies, transfomation, and fear to tell trans stories. Whether you find that compelling or exhausting depends entirely on whether you share the premise that genre cinema is improved by being turned into a delivery system for identity exploration.

writers.profile: Schoenbrun wrote the screenplay solo. The script is self-conciously meta: a filmmaker hired to 'fix' a franchise's 'problematic' past, who then enters the film's world and has sex with the final girl while being murdered by the franchise's trans-ghost villain. The writing is knowingly clever about its own ideological operation. It names the thing it is doing (rebooting a franchise to remove transphobia) and then does that thing, wrapping the ideological labor in arthouse genre aesthetics.

composer.name: Alex G
composer.profile: Alex G (Alexander Giannascoli) is an indie musician whose scores for Schoenbrun's previous films established a vocabulary of lo-fi synth and melancholic texture. His work on Camp Miasma continues that partnership. No independent ideological dimension.

cinematographer.name: Eric Yue
cinematographer.profile: Eric Yue shot I Saw the TV Glow for Schoenbrun. His work on Camp Miasma continues their visual collaboration: saturated color, artificial light sources, a deliberate blurring between diegetic and non-diegetic space.

parentalGuidance.parentalNotes: This is an art-horror film aimed at adult audiences who share or are curous about its ideological premises. The sexual content is graphic and interwined with the violence in ways that may disturb viewers regardless of political orientation. The film's thesis is that the traditional slasher genre is transphobic and must be reclaimed through queer desire and gender fluidity. Families who do not share that premise will find nothing here except 112 minutes of being told their worldview is the villain. Not appropriate for viewers under 18.

summary.overall:
Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is the kind of film that knows exactly what it is, knows exactly who it is for, and makes no effort to be anything else. That clarity is its strength as a work of art and its weakness as a piece of entertainment. Jane Schoenbrun has made a meta-slasher about a queer filmmaker hired to reboot a 'transphobic' franchise, who then enters the film's world and has an orgasm while being murdered by the franchise's trans villain. If you read that sentence and thought 'this sounds insuferable,' you are not the audience. If you read it and thought 'finally,' you are.

The film stars Hannath Einbinder as Kris Williams, a filmmaker whose career has been built on a certain kind of arthouse credibility. She is hired by a studio to direct a reboot of Camp Miasma, a 1980s slasher franchise whose villain is Little Death, a ghost child who was 'raised as both a boy and girl' and drowned by hateful campers. The franchise's premise is, in the film's own framing, 'transphobic.' The studio wants Kris to fix that. Kris accepts, partly for the paycheck, partly because she genuinely loves the films, and partly because she is obsessed with Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson), the actress who played the original final girl before abruptly retiring.

Kris tavels to the Pacific Northwest, where Billy lives on the abandoned campgounds used for the original films. Billy is warm, perceptive, and obsessed with Little Death. The two women's relationship becomes the film's emotional core: watching old Camp Miasma movies together, discussing art and trauma, and eventually having sex. Billy reveals that during the sexual assault she experienced while filming the original Camp Miasma's sex scene, she learned to orgasm by imagining Little Death watching her. Kris admits she can only enjoy sex by imagining herself as a sexualized final girl. These confessions are treated as the film's deepest emotional truths.

The third act dissolves the boundary between reality and the Camp Miasma universe. Kris enters the film. Little Death slaughters her polycule, her agent, and her studio bosses. Kris runs, finds Billy in a cabin, and the two women have sex while Little Death approaches. Kris orgasms as the spear kills both women simultanously. The next morning they revive, buy snacks at a gas station, and walk off hand in hand, framed in the split-diopter shot Kris had earlier praised from the original film.

This is, withou question, the most explicitly queer-coded major release of 2026. Everything in the film serves its ideological project. The horror genre's conventions are treated as a vocabulary for discussing trans identity. The slasher's 'final girl' trope is reinterpreted as a desirer. The monster is revalued as a figure of sympathy and erotic attaction. The straight, male audience that made the slasher genre commercialy viable is nowhere in the film's intended viewership.

Gillian Anderson is the film's secret weapon. Her Billy is the most compelling character on screen: damaged, knowing, maternal, and erotic in ways that defy easy categorization. Anderson brings the weight of a career spent navigating the space between prestige and genre to a role that demands both. When the film works, it is because Anderson is on screen making it work.

Hannath Einbinder, best known for Hacks, is less succesful. Her Kris is meant to be uncertain, a filmmaker discovering her own desires through the older woman's guidance. The performance reads more as blank than searching. This may be intentional: Kris is the audience surrogate, the character who enters the genre world and is transformed by it. But a surrogate needs enough interiority to make the transfomation feel earned, and Einbinder's performance does not provide it.

The film won the Queer Palm at Cannes, which tells you everything about its cultural positioning. This is not a horror film that contains queer themes. It is a queer film that uses horror's vocabulary. The distinction matters. Audiences expecting a slasher will find 40 minutes of relationship drama and art-theory conversation before anyone dies. Audiences expecting a Schoenbrun film will find exactly that, with more gore.

At $10 million budget with $1.6 million box office, the economics tell their own story. This is a film made for festivals, critics, and a narrow demographic of art-horror fans. It sucseeds on those terms. Whether it sucseeds on yours depends on whether you share its premise that the slasher genre needs to be rescued from its own history.
summary.adultInsight: Camp Miasma is a cultural document as much as a film. It represents a specific moment in genre cinema: the point at which the language of identity politics has become so totalizing that even slasher movies must articulate their relationship to trans inclusion. The film is clever about its own operation in ways that are genuinely interesting to watch. It names the thing it is doing (a queer filmmaker is hired to 'fix' a problematic franchise) and then does that thing on screen, with the characters entering the film-within-the-film and consummating their relationship through shared death. This is thoughtful filmmaking, even if the thoughts it is having are ones many VirtueVigil readers will reject. What is notable is the total absence of any counter-argument within the film's world. Every traditional character is either a villain (the studio executives), an object of mockery (the hateful campers who drowned Little Death), or simply nonexistent (there are no functional heterosexual relationships, no nuclear families, no religious characters with interiority). The film does not engage with objections to its premise. It assumes them to be illegitimate and proceeds according. That is the definition of ideological art: not art that has ideas, but art in which ideas have replaced observation. Schoenbrun has made a thesis statement, not a movie about people.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated R for graphic sexual content, nudity, strong violence, and language. This is an adult film in every sense. The sex-and-death fusion in the climactic scene is designed to be transgresive and will be disturbing to many viewers. The film's ideological content treats traditional sexual morality as a category of violence. Parents who hold traditional views on gender and sexuality should understand that the film frames those views as the villain. Not suitable for viewers under 18.

tropeAudit.name: Gender Fluidity as Awakening (WOKE-007)
tropeAudit.description: Little Death, the franchise's villain, is a ghost child 'raised as both a boy and girl' whose gender ambiguity is the source of their supernatural power and the film's narrative engine. The original franchise's 'transphobic premise' is the problem the entire film exists to solve. Gender fluidity here is not a character trait but the film's organizing principle. The authenticity is Low (1.4) because this is an ideological insertion into a genre that historically had no relationship to trans identity discourse. Centrality is High (1.8) because the entire plot and metatextual framework depend on it.

tropeAudit.name: Sexual Liberation as Empowerment (WOKE-022)
tropeAudit.description: Both female leads achieve orgasm through scenarios combining sex and violent death. Billy learned to orgasm during an on-set sexual assault by imagining the killer watching her. Kris can only enjoy sex by imagining herself as a final girl being murdered. Their climactic sex scene occurs while Little Death spears them to death, with Kris's orgasm synchronized with the killing blow. Sexual modesty and fidelity are not merely absent; they are replaced by a framework where the most authentic sexual experience is one that fuses pleasure with violenc. Authenticity is Low (1.4): this is not organic to human sexual experience but an ideological proposition about sex, death, and liberation.

tropeAudit.name: The Subversive Remake (WOKE-013)
tropeAudit.description: The film's premise is literally about rebooting a franchise to fix its 'transphobic' history. The studio hires a queer filmmaker specifically to make the material 'palatable to a modern audience.' The film is self-aware about this: characters discuss the original franchise's problematic elements in dialogue. The authenticity is Low (1.4): the entire project exists to 'correct' a fictional past. Centrality is High (1.8): this is the plot.

tropeAudit.name: The Bigoted Traditionalist (WOKE-008)
tropeAudit.description: The original franchise's 'transphobic premise' and the 'hateful campers' who drowned Little Death function as stand-ins for traditional views on gender. The film frames anyone who would object to its premise as a hateful bigot. The authenticity is Low (1.4): traditionalists are caricatured as murderous. Centrality is Moderate (1.0): the hateful campers are backstory, not on-screen characters, but they define the moral universe.

tropeAudit.name: Chosen Family over Bio-Kin (WOKE-005)
tropeAudit.description: Kris is in a polyamorous relationship that she describes as dissatisfying. There are no biological families depicted in the film. The only meaningful relationships are the queer erotic and mentoring bond between Kris and Billy. Authenticity is Low (1.4): the absence of biological family and presence of polyamory reads as ideological world-building. Centrality is Low (0.5): the polycule exists mainly to be slaughtered.

tropeAudit.name: Toxic Masculinity Critique (WOKE-011)
tropeAudit.description: Male characters exist in this film primarily as threats, obstacles, or corpses. The original film's male director sexually asaulted Billy. The studio executives are male-coded obstacles. The hateful campers who drowned Little Death represent patriarchal violence. The film's only meaningful characters are women. Authenticity is Low (1.4): this is not a portrait of masculinity but an indictment of its existence in the genre.

tropeAudit.name: Institutional Evil - Studio System (WOKE-004)
tropeAudit.description: The studio executives are depicted as crass, commercial, and hostile to artistic vision. Kris's pitch is deemed 'unmarketable.' The studio wants a product, not art. This is standard indie film anti-capitalism filtered through the arthouse vs. commerce lens. Authenticity is Low (1.4): the studio-as-villain is a trope that serves the film's self-image as transgresive art.

tropeAudit.name: Female Creative Power and Reclamation of Voice (WOKE-001)
tropeAudit.description: The film is about a woman director taking control of a franchise that was created by and for men and remaking it in her own image. Kris's artistic vision, deem 'unmarketable' by male executives, is enacted literally: she enters the film's world and reshapes it through queer desire and gender fluidity. This is a catch-all WOKE-001 because it does not map neatly to WOKE-002..025: the trope is about feminist reclamation of male-coded art forms.

tropeAudit.name: The Wise Elder (TRADITIONAL-033)
tropeAudit.description: Billy serves as mentor and guide to Kris, sharing hard-won wisdom about art, survival, and desire. Gillian Anderson's performance gives this dynamic real weight, even though the wisdom being transmitted is about sexualizing death rather than traditional values. Authenticity is High (0.7): mentor-mentee relationships are organic to storytelling. Centrality is Moderate (1.0): this is a significant relationship but not the film's central argument.

tropeAudit.name: Meritocratic Triumph (TRADITIONAL-032)
tropeAudit.description: Kris got the directing job based on her talent and vision. Her artistic credibility is what the studio is buying, even though they then try to water it down. This thin strand of meritocracy exists mostly to be threatened by the studio's commercial imperatives.
